en: Separate Record of National Teacher Yuanzhao, the First Patriarch of Huilin Chan Monastery at Da Xiangguo Temple in Tokyo (along with) Verses and Odes by Lingyan,
Abbot of Xiufeng Temple on Mount Lingyan in Suzhou.
Recorded by the Dharma-heir Wujì Dàshī Huìbiàn on the tenth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of Yuánfēng.
Emperor Zhézhōng summoned the Master into the palace.

At the Funing Hall, for the Imperial Carriage of Emperor Shenzong, after the Master had finished his expression of gratitude, he ascended the seat. Taking up the incense, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"This renowned incense is offered within the Funing Hall."
The Holy Sovereign has ordered the opening of the Buddha-field for selection. This is the personal entrustment from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. I, a monk, now proclaim it on his behalf.
Is there anyone here who will join me in exerting effort? At that time, a monk asked: "Within the Maitreya Pavilion, you discourse upon the wondrous Dharma."
[The student] said, "In the Lapis Lazuli Hall, the True Sect is performed. I do not know whether this is one or two. The Master said, "Two colors, one match.
[The student] further asked, "Without seeking out friends to the south, one sees Manjusri to the east. The Master said, "The dragon produces extraordinary colors; the lion hides its tracks.
[The student] further asked, "Its merit flows through ten thousand generations and remains ever-present; its Way penetrates a hundred kalpas and is ever more firm. The Master said, "Later..."
Viewing on the Fifth Day. A monk asked, "Within the nine-layered city, the true wind is widely spread;
the Sage’s intent gives rise to compassion—how may one repay it? The Master said, "Relying solely upon this day’s single burner of incense.
The monk further asked, "Not forgetting the record of the Vulture Peak in days of yore, how does the ancestral Way flourish once again? The Master replied, "It emerges."
The Emperor’s mind [was moved]. The Master said, “The true does not conceal the false; the crooked does not hide the straight.

[The Emperor] further asked, “It may be said that the mountains and rivers endure together for eternity, and the sun and moon provide joint testimony. The Master said, “Simply know how to do good deeds; there is no need to ask about your future path.
A monk asked, “In the past, when the Brahma King invited the Buddha, the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers. Today,” [he continued,] “...?”
The Emperor summoned the Master and asked, "What auspicious omens have there been? The Master replied, "Colorful clouds enshroud the Jade Palace; auspicious vapors shroud the incense in the burner.
The Emperor further said, "Heaven hangs down jeweled canopies, tier upon tier of elegance; the earth wells up golden lotuses, petal after petal of freshness.
The Master said, "Lift your eyebrows and quickly realize it! The Emperor further said, "As for this very..."
"The Imperial Majesty has offered sacrifices for the late Great Emperor. Where has the celestial carriage gone? The Master said, "It does not leave this very place; it is eternally serene.
The questioner continued, "In this realm his body has already passed away; in the Pure Land the nine lotuses have blossomed. The Master said, "This was already before words were spoken."
The Master then remained silent for a long while and said, "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? Indeed, the questions are inexhaustible and the answers are endless.
Why is this? The vehicle of the *zong* (essence) is vast and boundless; were it not for wondrous wisdom, its shores could not be fathomed. The path of the *xiang* (phenomena) is profound and subtle;

were it not for those of the highest capacity, its significance would rarely be exhausted. Truly, it may be said that within the luminous *dharmadhātu*, self and other, as well as object and wisdom, are fully encompassed.

The true source is vividly manifest; both self and other, as well as the holy and the mundane, are simultaneously stilled. Things and the self are in dark resonance; self and other meet in mutual penetration.
The Way is fundamentally thus, visible before one's eyes. The myriad phenomena of the universe fully reveal the ancestral style of the Buddhas;

the great earth and the heavens and earth everywhere manifest the crown-mark of Vairocana. The bells and drums of the six streets are the gateway through which Avalokiteśvara enters into principle. The jade palace of the moon...
Louvain. To expound upon this matter: if one can attain clear realization herein, then every thought-moment is Śākyamuni’s appearance in the world, and every step is Maitreya’s descent to be born.
The Master then looked toward those around him and said, "Do you understand? Why labor with subtle eloquence to proclaim it?"

What need is there to wait for supernatural powers to manifest this? If one can act in such a manner, they are worthy of repaying the unrequitable debt of gratitude and may join in assisting the transformation of the Unconditioned.
On this day, for the sake of the present Emperor, [we] reverently...

On the anniversary of the birth of the Great Emperor, one thousand monks were invited to observe a fast, and I, a humble monk, was specially summoned to ascend the seat and proclaim the Prajñāpāramitā.
By the merit thus accumulated, may it be dedicated to the late Emperor, the Immortal Sovereign.
We respectfully pray that he may transcend to the Pure Land, his numinous light remaining unclouded, and that he shall receive rebirth on the banks of the Sand-Gold Pond.

The gates of the jeweled pavilion of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* have opened; facing the countenance of Amitābha, they personally receive the Buddha’s prophecy and shall surely realize Bodhi.
May His Majesty the Emperor, who rules the realm, enjoy the blessings of a Cakravartin.
May longevity be attained to the point of brushing away the dust upon the rocks; may the myriad nations share in universal repose, and the Three Palaces flourish with abundant celebration.
May the Empress Dowager, the Empress Dowager, and the Imperial Consort Dowager alike find their blessings exceeding the vast ocean and their lifespans equaling Mount South.
May they dwell securely in the supreme dignity of the Earthly Pole, eternally receiving the sustenance of all under heaven, and remain long established.
May your holy compassion be ever-present; I humbly pray that you take care of yourself.

On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month of the eighth year of Yuanfeng, the Korean Monk-General Uichon, accompanied by the envoys Fan Sharen and Su Langzhong, entered Huilin Temple to visit the Master.

"I request an audience. The Sang-tong said, "Prince Uicheon, while in his own country, heard of your great fame. Having traveled far across the Eastern Sea, he specifically extends this prostration to pay homage.
Please, Master, take your seat and graciously accept these humble offerings. The Master replied, "We have never met face-to-face, nor do we share a teacher-disciple relationship;
how could I dare accept such worship? Although those around him earnestly entreated the Master to sit, he could not avoid it and thus sat down to receive the prostrations.
When he had finished, the Master asked the Sangha Superintendent, "I have heard that you have long been well-versed in the sutras and śāstras; is this true?

Tian replied, "I have applied my mind somewhat to the Great Teaching of the Avataṃsaka. The Master said, "Excellent. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra consists entirely of the profound discourse on the ultimate nature of reality, as revealed by all the sages."
“If one has not personally realized and awakened to it, it is difficult to clarify the wondrous principle of the *dharmadhātu*.
Have you ever had a point of entry into awakening? Tian said, “It is vividly manifest within the mind and eyes, yet its form cannot be seen.

The Master asked, “What is this that is vividly manifest within the mind and eyes? Tian said, “The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are all sealed by a single *dharma*. The Master said, “...”
"This is still merely words and language. What is this one Dharma? Tian said, "There is no place to open my mouth. The Master said, "You have not yet attained awakening.
The intent of all Buddhas is subtle and profound, majestic and manifest; if one has not entered through awakening, it is truly difficult to find words for it."
The Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one may become a Buddha. To see is simply to see;

it does not depend on deliberation, nor on written words, nor does it involve gradual stages. If one attempts to understand this through worldly wisdom or clever discernment, there is no such possibility.
Therefore, the Preface to the *Huayan fajie guan* says: "It is brilliantly manifest within the space between the heart and the eyes.
The Master looked at the Sengtong and said, "Excellent! If you can realize it here, it will be nothing short of extraordinary. He further said, "Yet its form cannot be seen."

Brilliantly manifest within the realm of form, yet its principle cannot be divided. Without the eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and the clear intelligence free from conceptual thought, one cannot see one’s own mind.
Such spiritual penetration is just as it is when spoken of in this way; but what, precisely, is this "own mind"? Tian said:
"The single word 'knowing' is the gate to all wonders. The Master said: "The single word 'knowing'..."
"How do you understand this? The Monk-Tong said, "I, Yitian, have never practiced Chan.
The Master said, "It would be like reaching a mountain of jewels and returning empty-handed. Yitian said, "A great spiritual friend is difficult to encounter even throughout kalpas.
The Master spoke again, "The single word 'knowing' is the gate to all wonders. At this point, can it be called Chan? Can it be called the Way? Is it not so?"
"The very place where it is raised—this is it. To set all aside at once, how do you understand this? Tian remained silent.
Then his companion, Fan Sheren, said, "As the ancients called it, 'The Way exists in a glance. The Master said, "I am right now with all of you."
They sat facing one another, gazing at each other; this may be called "witnessing with the eyes. [Tian asked: "What is the Way? Van Sharen replied, "It cannot be put into words.
The Master said, "If you say it cannot be put into words, that is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

The vast capacity of the Buddhas has produced the Great Canon of Teachings, exhausting every possible expedient means (*upāya*); how could it be that it cannot be put into words? The assembly was speechless. Tian bowed in thanks and withdrew.

In the first year of the Yuanyou era, on the first day of the third month, the State Preceptor of Goryeo requested the Master to ascend the seat. After the State Preceptor had finished offering incense, the Master said, "The affairs of the Buddha-dharma and human relations have both been concluded at once.
Nevertheless, though this is so, there is no harm in having questions and answers. At that time, a monk asked: "In the past..."
"At Caoxi for one night; at Longtan for one night. Today the Head of the Sangha has come briefly. I do not know whether these are the same or different.
The Master said, "It can be verified right before your eyes. The monk stepped forward and said, "I thought the news of Shaolin had been cut off, yet now its traces remain clearly present.
The Master said, "As for the single phrase of Caoxi, how would you say it? The monk replied, "Where there is water, it all contains the moon."
"There is no mountain that does not carry clouds. The Master said, "It may be so, but what can one do about explaining the principle?
The student advanced and said, "If you will not explain the principle, then please let the Master speak. The Master said, "Quickly, prostrate three times."
A monk asked, "The ancient sages said: 'Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams, seeking teachers and visiting paths for the sake of Zen.

Please, Master, bestow upon me that one phrase for the moment of departure. The Master said, "Listen attentively, listen attentively. The monk stepped forward and said, "The solitary radiance is without partiality;

its proclamation is according to the standard. The Master said, "Henceforth, you must not speak of this erroneously. The monk stepped forward and said, "Do not say that those in the assembly do not recognize it—[it is] solitary..."
The bright solitary shadow projects upon the empty hall. The Master said, "It is not as good as prostrating. A monk asked, "I do not ask about coming from ten thousand miles away to pay court;

but what is the meaning of unfurling the sails and turning the oars? The Master said, "Wash your feet and then board the boat. The monk pressed further, "Drawing the sleeve back, one brushes away the rain from the dragon cave;
raising the cup, the waves surge and the lotuses bloom in the alms-bowl. The Master said, "What is the phrase for reaching the shore?"
Daojin said, "Had it not been for the State Preceptor coming to visit me, how could the Master have brought forth this teaching again? The Master said, "I do not yet dare grant you that.
The Master then continued, "According to the fundamental way of meeting face-to-face under the ancestral gate, it does not depend on ascending the Dharma seat or unfolding [the robe]."

Why do I expose these sharp words? Even if Huelin possessed the fourfold unimpeded eloquence, when the mechanism of a sudden thunderclap reaches before you all, not a single point of it would be of any use.
Why is this so? Furthermore, each and every one of you possesses a majestic radiance that illuminates heaven and earth;
everyone has the *śakrāksa* (Śakra-eye) that firmly grasps heaven and earth and remains continuous without leaking.
Encompassing the present and shrouding the past, it is as impenetrable as water-tight sealing. It cuts off the stream of birth and death and occupies the seat of the patriarchs and Buddhas.

Wondrous, perfect, and transcendent—this is precisely the moment. O virtuous ones, if you can attain clarity in this place, you may be said to have attained the Dharma-body without passing through kalpas of monastic training.
Even so, this is still but a tangle of vines. If one were to act according to the Patriarchal Command, then at the mere lift of an eye, a thousand [barriers]...

Mountains ten thousand and waters a hundred. To deliberate upon them is like the vast distance between heaven and earth; what more need be said? The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has not reached this day.

Let us set aside these matters for now. On this day, I am deeply honored that the Attendant-in-Ordinary, together with the Great Master, the State Preceptor of Goryeo, entered the temple to offer incense and earnestly requested me to ascend the seat. Moreover—

The Great Master, the Sang-tong, possessed merit in the past and possessed the power of vows in the past. Had his past merit not been profound and deep, by what cause would he have been born into a royal family?
Had his vow-power not been firm and steadfast, by what cause would he have suddenly renounced worldly glory and nobility to don the dharma robes?
Therefore, his innate disposition was lofty and far-reaching, and as a vessel of the Dharma, he was perfectly formed; he was able to propagate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra in his own country.

The teachings have already established their grand framework; yet, he did not shrink from the vast distance of ten thousand *li*, braving the surging waves to travel afar in search of further masters.
He exhaustively investigated the profound and abstruse depths, becoming a dragon among the scales of the ocean of teachings for this final age.

To interpret the celestial phenomena of the Śākya stars—who else but the *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Sangha) could have accomplished this? Truly, such a person is one who cannot easily be found. However, as for the Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*...

This is inconceivable; it is the ultimate discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), intended solely for those of superior capacity. It is like the sun shining alone upon a high mountain;
it does not even enter the hands of those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). To thus exert all effort in its propagation—how could this be for a minor cause?

When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, first attained perfect enlightenment, he beheld that all sentient beings were profoundly deluded and ignorant regarding the vast and great *dharmadhātu*, and were unable to...
Although they possess self-realization and vast majestic power, they are unable to employ them. Therefore, the Tathāgata sighed, saying: "How marvelous!
I now see that all sentient beings universally possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, because of their attachment to deluded thoughts, they do not realize or attain them.
Thereupon, across the seven locations and nine assemblies, he spoke exhaustively according to the nature of the Dharma-realm, until—
The superior version consists of as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms;
the middling version consists of as many verses as there are atoms in one four-continent world system; and even the inferior version still contains hundreds of thousands of sublime stanzas.

These constitute the Great Teaching obtained here in Jambudvīpa, intended to enable sentient beings throughout the ten directions to realize that they themselves possess the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Wisdom contains the Dharma-realm within a single atom; it universally perceives the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) within all lands. One and many are without obstruction; the large and small are perfectly interfused.
Casting the great trichiliocosm beyond the four quarters, one receives Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed—all this is the constant nature of sentient beings;
wherever there is mind, it is thus. Yet, since they possess mind, why do they not see it? Therefore, we know that if it were not for...
The eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and the brilliant intelligence free from conceptual thought cannot see [this] by themselves. Yet, if one were to see it, it would be as follows:

it has no form or appearance, yet it pervades the great chiliocosm; it has no boundaries, yet it encompasses all existence. It is so in every thought-moment, in every particle of dust, and in every phenomenon.
Throughout the past and present, the coming and going of time, the large and the small, the internal and the external—not even a hair’s breadth is moved.
There is no sign of disparity; they penetrate one another in successive layers, interlacing like a celestial net.

Although it is thus, this remains the Dharma-realm of perfect fusion—a description of its meaning through words and signs. Within this context, how do you understand "a single mote of dust containing the entire Dharma-realm"?
"To have attained this within this assembly can be called swallowing the entire teaching of a lifetime in a single gulp.
He then let out a shout and said, "It is better to understand the meaning of this one shout. As it is clearly stated in the sutras:

"The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates is fully expressed in a single word, leaving nothing behind. Thirty years hence, do not fail Huelin. The Monastic Head (Sengtong) bowed in thanks to the Master.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Who, upon ten thousand acres of vast waves, For the sake of the Dharma forgets their own body to emulate Sudhana? I imagine such a person is rare indeed in Jambudvīpa;
It is like an udumbara flower blooming amidst fire. Having spoken thus, he descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "If we speak according to the fundamental approach of our ancestral lineage, seeing one another in the true sense does not depend on ascending the Dharma seat to display the sharp edge of speech.
Why is this? It is for this reason it is said: 'If the sharp edge of speech errs, the homeland is ten thousand miles away.

One must let go completely from the precipice and take responsibility for oneself; only then can one revive after death, for nothing can deceive the Honored One. Therefore, the former sages skillfully opened [the way]."
Skillful means thus unfolds through many gates, established upon the foundation of non-abiding. Since the foundation itself is non-abiding, it can respond to manifold conditions.

It is like a great bell suspended on its frame, manifesting sound according to the strike; or like the bright moon casting its radiance, universally responding as it is reflected in a thousand rivers.
These are all instances of unconditioned compassion, responding to stimuli according to the capacity of beings. This is the principle of non-duality, which follows...
The capacities of sentient beings are distinguished by their mutual differences; though the teachings follow many paths, their principle returns to a single convergence.

Sometimes realization is attained at the tip of the staff: striking the meditation seat with a staff, he says, "Directly realize it right here! Or, taking responsibility upon a shout, he lets out a roar and asks, "Do you understand?
When thought and expression race against one another, they are equally like drifting currents; when phenomena and principle are seen as uniform, one suddenly beholds the Tathāgata.
He uproots the deep-seated roots of birth and death and attains the samādhi of presence. How much more so for this Great Way, which is manifest and clear, its wondrous principle subtle and profound;
where numinous wisdom appears before one, flowing freely in application. Again, looking left and right, he said: "Look! Look!

If you can attain clarity at this very point, then mind after mind will be eternally quiescent, and phenomenon after phenomenon will be spiritually penetrating. There will be no need to laboriously seek it."
Half a verse was used to sacrifice one's entire body, yet it could not be obtained; this is because birth and death serve as the cause, and suffering and pleasure act as the root.

Without awakening to the true permanence, how can one penetrate the sublime purport? The floating world is tumultuous, and throughout the day one remains in a state of dullness, entangled by the consciousness of karma.

One has not yet attained sudden awakening; however, if one can simply turn the light back with single-mindedness, that itself is the matter of transcending the mundane. To speak in such a way is also a tangle of complications.
When examined thoroughly, it is truly ten thousand miles of white clouds. I have stood for a long time before you, O compassionate assembly; I humbly pray that you will all take care of yourselves.
Ascending the hall, after the monks had finished their questions, the Master said: "The questions are inexhaustible, and the answers are likewise endless.
If we speak of curing illness, there is no need for medicine to be carried on a donkey. Why is this? The sages of old transmitted but a single word or half a phrase;

they did so only because they could not help it, out of necessity. To explain various heterodox views at length would be utterly contrary to the essence of the Way, let alone when it comes to the Subtle."
Transcending all phenomena, its principle governs all directions; it immediately manifests through manifold gates while its radiance enshrouds the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Inferring from this, the Way is realized through the mind and does not reside in words and language. It is profound and majestic, never interrupted. Without exerting the intellect or will, simply turn the light back upon itself for a moment;
then daily life is fully encompassed, and how could "self" and "other" possibly stand apart? Thus it is said: "Throughout the entire universe and pervading the Dharma-realm."

All that comes forth is merely a realm of delusion. Apart from the sudden awakening to the True Vehicle, establishing a profound path, utterly forgetting subject and object, realizing the fundamental absence of mind, discerning and shattering worldly toil, and clearly identifying the factions of Māra—if one can understand it in this way, [then one has attained it].

"What a joy for my entire life! If you have not yet understood this, it is simply because you yourselves are avoiding it. [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his staff and descended from the seat.
He then ascended the hall and said: "Excellent, O virtuous Chan practitioners! Strike the Dharma drum three times and expound the inexhaustible Dharma gates. His attendant...

As for this offering of incense: these successive acts of Buddha-work, if considered from the standpoint of the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), cannot be proclaimed by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, nor can they be established by the six generations of patriarchs.
If considered from the standpoint of the gate of Buddha-work, one must rely on pointing and indicating;
thus, there is a Buddha-land in every speck of dust and a Śākyamuni in every leaf, like the pearls hanging from a celestial net—within this Dharma-gate, there is no...
Thus, at the eastern outskirts of the city of Awakening, the youth Sudhana beheld Mañjuśrī from afar;
he then ascended Mount Mārgaṇa and subsequently traveled southward, visiting spiritual friends throughout one hundred and ten cities until finally arriving before the Great Pavilion.

He then saw Maitreya, who said: "I have already first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva conduct, nor how one cultivates the bodhisattva path. Maitreya snapped his fingers once;
there was not even a single trace left. Sudhana then asked: "Noble One, where has that magnificent array you displayed just now gone?"
Maitreya said, "He has gone from where he came. Therefore it is said: "The luminous Flower Treasury realm, before one's eyes, is utterly free of even a speck of dust.
Here and there is Maitreya; no gate, no Sudhana. Transversely and vertically, they distinguish the principal and the attendant; interchanging, they reveal the towers and pavilions.
If you begin to set up conceptual deliberation to look at them, from where would such adornments come? The Master again called to the assembly, "The very last..."
"A phrase! No monk under heaven can leap out of it. He then descended from his seat.
The Great King of Jing personally brought the title "Chan Master Yuanzhao" to him and offered this verse in thanks:
"The power of heaven and earth cannot exhaust it; In impartial governance, who has greater merit? How shall the sons of Śākya repay the grace they receive?"
Response. A Prayer at the White Sandalwood Incense Burner for the Wind of Yao’s Virtue.
Twenty Verses on Dwelling at Lingyan Mountain:
Upon the elegant Lingfeng Peak, The dust is still and the summer feels cold. Pine and vines spread across the emerald ridges; Pagodas and halls tower above the clouds.
The mountain caves have high and low entrances; the paths to the mountain lodgings wind and turn. Their midst is truly secluded and hidden—why need one gaze upon painted scrolls?
Leading my steps to the edge of the western crags, I lean on my staff for a single look: the waters of Lake Tai flow on and on, and Mount Dongting looms far and deep.
The wind carries the cloud-sailed boat far away; as the mist clears, the scene becomes tranquil. At evening, atop the pine treetops, a hundred herons return with their catch of fish.
By nature I love to dwell in the mountains, always longing for the edge of water and rock. Fortunate to live at the dawn of this clear age, I remain in high seclusion before the wondrous peak.
Drinking from the Way, I pass my days in leisure; dwelling the spirit, years are not counted. In solitude, I find joy only for myself; lacking worldly merit, I benefit neither humans nor devas.
Since arriving to dwell among the mountains, suddenly three or four autumns have passed. I pay no heed to the human world; beyond all things, I have severed all pursuit and wandering.
My worn robes are patched as needed; for my alms, I seek them as they come. With nothing extra upon this single body, I sit alone, my thoughts drifting on.
All say that dwelling in the mountains is good, yet the affairs of mountain life are difficult. If even a fragment of the mind has not ceased its activity, how can one find peace within?

In the ninth month of summer, how could there be no heat? In the third month of winter, how could it not be cold? If one can clearly understand this principle, we may linger together beneath the pine trees.
The site where the Ruler of Wu once built his palace remains with its lakes and mountains still as they were. Though rise and fall differ in their course, the wind and moon have never changed.
My eyes touch upon past events; my grieving heart recalls the sages of old. In their petty toil they followed the flowing waters; who among them has returned again through the ages?
To dwell in the mountains without seeing the mountains—only then is one truly dwelling in the mountains. Until one reaches the groundless mind, it is difficult to attain the ease of true realization.
Flowers bloom amidst the green ridges; cranes cry out between the white clouds. No one understands this meaning; all day long I keep the gate closed alone.
Once I have ascended the cloud-covered peak, I shall never descend from its perilous summit. Far removed from the red dust of the world, I dwell deep within the borders of the emerald mountains.
Benefiting sentient beings has now ceased; I lie high upon my bed, following conditions as they arise. If you ask by what artifice I rely, it is the *kāṣāya*, the field of merit.

Retreating into seclusion to dwell among crags and valleys, I hide deeply, claiming to have attained the Way. I pay no heed at all to worldly ties; what further schemes for mundane affairs could there be?
The mind rests quietly at the profound pass; with feelings stilled, this Way is extraordinary. Sitting in silent seclusion within the hermitage, I face only a sandalwood incense burner.
The celestial sphere sustains the four phases; time and light flow as swiftly as a current. How can worldly conditions endure? How many autumns does human life possess?
What prevents one from resting by the pines and rocks? Let us find our peace amidst the waters and clouds. Avoid the toil that fills one’s head with white hair within the red dust of the world.
The majestic peaks of Lingyan rise in formidable grandeur; as they have been since ancient times, they do not change. Those who travel north and south can only gaze upward in admiration;
how few have actually reached the summit and walked there?
Lingyan is pure and vast, utterly free from the clamor of the world; this entire realm is so serene it seems more real than a painting.
What is most wonderful within it is that the myriad phenomena are ever new throughout the four seasons.
From afar, the four quarters behold the towering majesty of Lingyan. As mist unrolls and clouds disperse, the emerald crags unfold.
This realm is serene and secluded, entirely beyond the mundane world; since Sudhana departed, who else has come?
The sacred traces of Lingyan are wondrous and inexhaustible; Jizhi himself came to transform this place. Standing alone with fists raised—do you understand?
Kāśyapa’s smile is of the same wind.
The majestic peaks of Lingyan rise loftily, unsurpassed; the surrounding crags on all four sides dare not obstruct them.
At times, white clouds drift away from here, becoming rain for the fields or canopies for the earth, spreading across the ends of the world.
The ancient temple of Lingyan presses against the clouds; the road is perilous, and even for those who reach it, entry is difficult.
Only the travelers from the five lakes, whose lives are like drifting clouds and water, carry their jars and staffs together to find peace within these walls.
Sitting alone at Lingyan when the night is deep, the fire is cold and the ashes are chill—only I know this. For now, I maintain my solitude according to my lot;
the constant radiance is uninterrupted, which is itself non-action.
The sublime realm of Lingyan is wondrous beyond thought; only those who know it realize its great compassion. The breadth of its monastic tradition is unfathomable to men;
dragons and snakes mingle together in a single assembly.

Mount Lingyan is no different from Vulture Peak; it is simply that people of this age do not see it before them. If one can personally realize this in the face of it, why need one go out of one's way to seek the West?

A few verses on Lingyan are spoken briefly; yet even according to these, much remains untransmitted. If one asks the mountain elder what he has to say, not even the wondrous gāthās as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could proclaim it.
On New Year’s Day in the mountains, I have avoided worldly affairs.

These two verses are to inform you, my dark-clad disciples, that you may cease your New Year greetings. Leaving the household life is not comparable to remaining at home; I, this old monk, shall personally observe the events of my own life.
Seventy years have passed like a single dream.

I say to myself that dwelling in the mountains allows me to escape idleness; why then exhaust my mind and strength to celebrate the New Year? A lifespan of hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of years is but a matter of this single morning;
the phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness pass in the snap of a finger.
The Lady Guo commissioned an image of Avalokiteśvara and requested that I compose a hymn for it:
O Auspicious One atop Mount Potalaka, Your wondrous features and true grace pervade as many worlds as motes of dust. With eyes of compassion, you universally observe all within the three realms;
With a heart of mercy, you extensively save all, regardless of kin or stranger.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Master Tiānyī:
The true countenance of the Teacher manifests boundlessly according to conditions; like the moon’s reflection upon a thousand rivers, its radiance is not of two kinds.
Sent to an Elder to reside at Benjue Monastery in Xiuzhou.
This old monk is advanced in years and already limping; I rely solely on you, my son, to uphold the vigorous tradition of our school. When people of Jiahe ask for the true news, tell them:
Lingyan Mountain lies amidst the white clouds.
I send Elder Yuan to reside at Shousheng Temple in Wuxi;
his son now wishes to depart to continue our lineage. Raising the eyebrows, he stands in the wind; in his great function, there is no need to be constrained by the favorable or the adverse.
From the tip of the staff, inexhaustible thought flows forth.
Seeing Elder Zhou take up residence at Ling’an Gongchen:

Relying on conditions as they arise, let things flow naturally; there is no need for haste. To be without mind regarding all affairs is the wondrous remedy. Sitting idly in stillness, people cannot fathom it;
Spontaneously, a divine light radiates from behind the crown of his head.
I see Elder Qi departing for Anle Mountain in Yuhang;

for ten years we dwelt together in the temple by the lake. We explored the profound mysteries and exhausted the teachings, mutually supporting one another. Now you hold high the ancestral seal, transcending all others;
you are well-suited to serve as a guide for devas and humans.
Written while studying the Way before Elder Xun at Mount Huiri in Fuzhou: A single word once accorded with the pivot of the Patriarchs;
Now, having continued the lineage after the Transmission of the Lamp, May our school attain an inexhaustible future.

To Elder Yi of Langshan in Tongzhou, who has heard that his disciple already dwells atop Chicken Ridge: What business brings you across the river this morning? You have not forgotten the instructions of the Vulture Peak;
meeting Mañjuśrī once again, you emulate Sudhana.
To Li Gongbao:
After this realization, though you may have no further concerns, you must still refine yourself from time to time. When stains and defilements are completely removed, the whole body is revealed;
its radiance transcends the three realms, and none can surpass it.
To Li, the Inspector:

I urge you to cultivate the Way and do not be negligent. Swiftly passing time does not wait for anyone; you must frequently examine yourself within the present moment, so that in this very life you may attain the body of Śākyamuni.
To Li Yudai: You have already realized the treasure within yourself. Deeply concealed in the spiritual treasury, how could it be easily displayed? The former masters called it a priceless jewel;
every time it is brought forth, it is ever new.
To Li Chaofeng:
When this old monk first arrived at Huilin, you alone were esteemed by the assembly. If one applies oneself with equal diligence, one must penetrate to the ultimate;
even the Patriarchs were but men of the world.
Entrusted to Li Tongzhi:
You should uphold the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs well; do not allow any lapses to occur within your time. A single expanse, serene and still, is neither internal nor external;
it flows continuously without leakage until one reaches the state of non-action.
Entrusting this to the Prince of Zhaoxuan of the Liang Dynasty:
In years past, for three years I resided at Huilin Temple. Relying solely on your great power, the grace you bestowed was profound. Now that I am beneath these trees, how shall I repay you?
I shall simply add more "shore-sea" incense to the burner from time to time.

I write to you, Lady Liu, regarding how things are going at the hermitage behind your residence. I imagine you spend much of your time reading scriptures and reciting the Buddha’s name. As days turn into years, your merit will naturally flourish;
what need is there to envy the old woman of Zhaozhou?
To Professor Lǚqiū, formerly the Great Officer Lù of Nánquán: The Way has been transmitted for a thousand ages and spread throughout Jambudvīpa.
Now that you have already understood the meaning of the Western Arrival, You share the same path as those of that time.

I tell you, Master Chen Xianyuan, that you have now awakened to the pivot of the Patriarch’s teaching. You should skillfully apply this within the midst of daily activity. Every glance is nothing other than the Flower Treasury World;
transcending both ordinary and sagely realms occurs in an instant.
At Chōshō-an, dwelling in the mountains on a mid-autumn night, it was again the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival. Looking far across the vast sky, the moon was perfectly full.
How wonderful it was, walking alone and sitting alone by myself upon the pine and rocks before the hermitage, in perfect peace and ease.
The verse reveals Yongjia’s Compassionate Illumination;
his merit is so lofty it has no peer. He contemplates all sentient beings with equanimity as they encounter conditions everywhere.
Having clarified the mind-ground as universally unimpeded, its daily functioning flows freely and ceaselessly.
Having heard that Cizhao resides in seclusion, I send this verse to him:

The Great Recluse dwells amidst the marketplace, having constructed a bamboo hermitage; it is already known that the Abbot studied under [Mazu] in his youth. I imagine he must have reached a state of profound, unadulterated purity.
Yet, one must laugh at Master Lu’s insistence on pointing the way southward.

Manifesting perfect illumination, it illuminates the ten directions without interior or exterior. The numinous light shines alone, beyond surpassing. The Pure Land is but the mind; there is no coming or going.
To be in accord with this moment after moment is to be a Buddha.

Revealing the light of wisdom, he raises up clearly the heart-mind of the ancient Buddhas; from this, the sages of old awakened to the perfect sound. If one can simply have deep faith, one will surely attain it in the end;
the ultimate Way is not difficult—it is not separate from the present moment.
The Assistant Magistrate Lü Six requested an explanation of causes and conditions. [The Master] showed him this verse:
"The mind itself is the Buddha and the Teacher; the ancient sages have never transmitted anything different from this. A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends billions of worlds;
the Buddhas of the ten directions share this same condition."
At the residence of Grand Preceptor Lü, each person requested a Dharma name. To show them [the meaning], he presented it in verse:
"The Dharma name is Juecheng (Awakened Clarity). It is tranquil beyond compare, like the autumnal moon disc, its light shining upon the myriad waters."
The Dharma is named Universal Awakening; all myriad conditions are completely pared away, and the divine pearl alone remains, its numinous light shining brightly.
The Dharma is named Universal Response; it functions spontaneously without fixed form, yet amidst the myriad images and thousand shapes, there is only the wondrous nature of clarity.
The Dharma is named "Awakened Existence. It is pure and unattached, carefree beyond all things, like clouds or a crane.
The Dharma is named "Eternal Awakening. The divine pearl is never obscured; it illuminates the past and soars through the present, its radiance having neither interior nor exterior.
The Dharma is named "Skillful Penetration"; its transformations are inexhaustible, appearing and disappearing like clouds following a dragon.
The Dharma is named "Fixed Radiance"; day and night without interval, the myriad phenomena are arrayed within it, their reflections manifest therein.
The Dharma is named "Excellence in Illumination" (Shanming). It reflects upon both the present and the past; sentient and insentient beings alike dwell within the Pure Land.
The Dharma is named "Excellence in Tranquility" (Shanning). "Tranquility" means peaceful stillness. Seated before the myriad phenomena of the universe, the mind rests at ease within a single realm.
The Dharma is named "Prior Awakening"; it does not wait for the capacity of the recipient to arise later. When the Great Function manifests before one, the crow flies and the hare runs.
The newly appointed Governor of Dingzhou, Secretary Lü, bestowed upon me a seamless *kāṣāya*. I have therefore composed this verse to express my gratitude.
This seamless *kāṣāya* is truly difficult to obtain; it has traveled from afar, arriving without waiting even for Maitreya.

Seeing off the Zen practitioner Chief Seat Keum as he departs from me to return to Dongyue: Walking alone through clouds and mountains, how lofty and pure! In the deep night of one’s native land, who will share this view?
The Mirror Lake contains the autumn moon for ten thousand ages.
I send forth the Zen practitioner Qingli;
this old monk requires only that his realization be perfected. Once attained, he may proceed as he pleases in whatever direction.
If you can go hence and transmit the ancestral seal, skillfully opening up expedient means to benefit all sentient beings.
I sent Zhaoruzana up to Lingyan Mountain several years ago to study the Way; it was only after his realization that I came to know how supreme this matter is.
He strides with lofty steps toward Vairocana, traveling north and south, while his *śakara* eyes illuminate heaven and earth.
Transmitting the light of the Dharma,

the masters of the ten directions transmit together the mind of the ancient Buddhas; from the entrustment at Vulture Peak until the present day, the dark-clad disciples desire to continue this with lofty resolve,
and wherever they stand, they must cause all to look up in reverence.

I see the Dharma Master Yuan, a disciple in patched robes, take his leave and descend from the Verdant Heights. Entering the marketplace to transform and guide others, he must act according to the occasion.
Only by being able to protect the treasure within his robe can he exercise great compassion as inexhaustibly as the sun and moon.
Seeing off Master Ruan, the patriarch-monk was originally without any fixed abode; with his single staff he drifted away, unable to be detained.
If you encounter people on the road who ask for news of him, respond to their inquiry with words that precede sound and follow speech.
Seeing off Master Bianhua:

A gentle breeze sweeps across as the waters flow on and on. The thousand peaks stretch to the horizon, their emerald hues seeming to stream forth. When the time is right, the patch-robed monk departs following his inspiration;
amidst the convergence of myriad concerns, he offers a single word in response.
I bid farewell to the Chan disciple Jinghuazhu:
in studying the Way, do not shrink from toil. Among those in this world, none are not lofty who possess the Way. How could the sages of antiquity have attained it so easily?
They sacrificed their bodies for the Dharma as if they were but a speck of dust or a hair.
I bid farewell to the Elder Master Jiaohua;
as he is unable to proceed with his various duties, he shall remain at Lingyan to recuperate from his illness. As for the guidance of others, I have already entrusted this to my Zen disciples;
may they skillfully transmit the mind-seal throughout the world.
Seeing off Master Yuan as he returns to Deqing, his son comes to inquire about the Way;
past affinities are pursued through the ancestral intent, which relies solely upon the highest capacity. To return in a single night is still considered dull;
those who beckon across the river are rare indeed.
To Xie Zhuming, Censor-in-Chief. Two Poems.
Precious tea and fine verses were sent from afar; Opening the bag, I see they have been resealed. The high officials’ esteem is profound, yet I lack the means to repay it;
I gaze up at the celestial path, separated by ten thousand peaks.
Gain and loss are two ends of human affairs; rely on you to examine them with careful reflection. The power and influence of heroes are but a dream of the Southern Branch;
viewed from this perspective, they are all the same.
I tell you, young scholar Chen:

whether one follows the path of Confucianism or Buddhism, each proceeds according to their own merit. The Way resides in the realm of non-being; though the destinations differ, you are heading toward the clouds and mists to pluck the immortal cassia from the heights, while I, an old monk, seek only the stillness of solitude.
When the Dragon Girl presented her precious pearl at Vulture Peak, she manifested the wisdom of a bhikṣuṇī and immediately ascended to the fruit of Buddhahood in a mere instant.
Since you now understand the dharma of non-arising, you are no different from those of that time.

Two Poems for the Junior Disciple Huiju At the age of eight, a youth from some family, He sought out a teacher to leave the household life. Before the Buddha he repeatedly bowed his head, And often, flowers fell from the heavens.
Entering the Gate of Emptiness in my youth, I possessed the power of vows from previous lives. If one can maintain a firm and steadfast mind, benefit will be accomplished over a long duration.

Because a Zen practitioner painted my portrait, I am requested to compose a verse for this old man whose hair is like snow. With nimble hands, you have skillfully transmitted my ugliness and clumsiness; let it be hung upon the high wall of the Pine Hall.
A moment later, it was as if one were facing the moon over the autumn river in its solitary stillness.
Wen Chaofeng produced the "Diagram of the Patriarchs of Xuefeng" and presented it, requesting a eulogy:
"Towering is Xuefeng, manifesting his transformation like a dragon. To gaze upon him is inexhaustible; to look up to him is majestic. Truly extraordinary!"
A month has passed in the vast void.

To show Zhou Chengyi that the emerald caverns are steep and rugged, with few who reach them, you, Master Cheng, have come up the mountain along the path. With a single word, Caoxi is already understood.
The Essential Meaning: "The boundless clouds of delusion are cleared away by a single shout.
My junior disciple Shuzi seeks Amida Buddha;
he requests that I praise the wondrous form of Amida, whose merit is immeasurable. I hereby entrust this to Shuzi, to be used forever for offerings.
In the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era,
Emperor Shenzong issued an imperial decree summoning Chan Master Yuanzhao to serve as the abbot of HuiLin Chan Monastery. In the third month of the first year of the Yuanyou era,
he obtained permission to retire from HuiLin.
Emperor Zhezong issued an edict stating that monasteries were not permitted to compel the abbot to remain, allowing him to travel freely as he pleased.
The Master retired to Lingyan Mountain, where he stayed for twelve years. During his leisure time, he occasionally composed songs and verses at the request of others;
this was one manifestation of our Master’s compassionate grace. In the second year of the Yuanyu era, the tenth...
On the twenty-eighth day of the second month, he passed away peacefully while sitting upright without illness.
On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the following year, he was buried on the summit of this mountain above the Yan-shi Pond. In the fifth month of the second year of the Chongning era.
The present Emperor has issued an imperial decree bestowing the posthumous title "Chan Master Fākōng" upon him and granting his stupa the name "Stupa of Auspicious Light.

Furthermore, one monk shall be ordained each year to maintain the incense and lamps. Alas! The virtue and conduct of this Master were esteemed with such profound reverence by both the sagacious sovereign and his worthy ministers.

His grace was extraordinary. Aside from the records of his discourses at the three monastic centers of Shuiguang, Jingci, and Huiyin, which have already been printed and circulated in the world, Huibian now, in commemoration of his late master’s legacy, has compiled the sermons and verses from Huiyin and Lingyan that had not yet been carved into printing blocks. These are hereby assembled.
Postscript: I, Zhu Qin, serving as Acting Jangshi Lang, commissioned artisans to carve and print this work so that it might not fall into oblivion.
Recorded respectfully on the third day of the third month in the third year of the Daguan era.
At Jingde Lingyin Chan Monastery in Hangzhou, the junior disciple and master of the abbot, Shouyi Fazhen, has edited this work.
It is appended here as a successor to the lineage of Chan Master Tianyi Zongzheng Yihuai (the fifth generation of Yunmen).
Chan Master Yuanzhao Zongben of Hui-lin Temple in Tokyo was a native of Wuxi in Changzhou. His clan name was Guan. He was of robust and imposing stature, and his character was simple and sincere.
At the age of nineteen, he went to Chengtian Temple in Gusu and relied upon Chan Master Daosheng of Yong’an.

He performed the tasks of pounding grain and cooking, never growing weary or resentful. Whenever Daosheng entered the room for private instruction, he would join the assembly in seeking guidance. Daosheng said: "The Way..."
"Exerting yourself to such an extent, have you experienced any fatigue? The Master said, "If one were to abandon even a single dharma, it could not be called the fulfillment of Bodhi.
Since I truly desire to realize this in my present body, what fatigue could there be? Yang Qi was struck with wonder by this.

Ten years later, he shaved his head, received the full precepts, and served the Master as an attendant for another three years. Then, requesting leave to travel, he went to Chiyang and visited Tianyi at Jingde Temple.
[The Master] raised his robe. As Vasubandhu descended from Maitreya’s inner palace, Asaṅga asked: "Four hundred years among humans constitute a single day and night for those devas.
During one such period, Maitreya brings five hundred billion devaputras to fulfillment and causes them to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
I wonder what dharma he preaches? Vasubandhu replied: "He is preaching precisely this very dharma. It is as follows:
"What is this Dharma? he asked. After a long time, he attained enlightenment. One day, while in the master's room, he asked, "What is it like when 'this very mind is Buddha'?
The master replied, "What difficulty is there in killing people and setting fires? Thereupon, his fame spread throughout the world.

The Transport Commissioner, Lord Li Fugui, commissioned the master to open the Dharma at Rui Guang Monastery, where the assembly grew increasingly flourishing daily. Then, Lord Chen Xiang, the Governor of Wulin, [invited him...]
The Emperor commanded the Master to choose between the two monasteries of Chengtian and Xingjiao; however, the people of Suzhou crowded the roads to detain him.

Furthermore, due to the persistent invitation from Jingci Monastery, he issued a formal letter to inform the clergy and laity, saying: "I borrow the Master for three years to plant the seeds of merit for this region;
I dare not occupy him for long. Only then did the clergy and laity comply. In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, Emperor Shenzong issued an edict to expand the Xiangguosi Monastery.
There were sixty-four monasteries, organized into eight divisions: two for Chan and two for Vinaya. The Emperor summoned the Master and appointed him as the first patriarch of Hui-lin Monastery.

Upon his arrival, the Emperor dispatched an envoy to inquire after his well-being. After three days had passed, an imperial edict was proclaimed for the Master to expound the Dharma at the three gates of the monastery for the sake of the officials and the common people.
On the following day, he was summoned for an audience at the Yanhe Hall, where he was granted a seat; the Master then sat with his legs folded in the lotus position.

As he was about to collapse, the Emperor hurriedly ordered his close attendants to provide him with two additional brocade seats. When the Shenzong Emperor passed away, [the Master] was summoned to the Funing Hall to preach the Dharma.
Requesting to retire to the forest due to his old age, he received an imperial decree allowing him to wander freely as he pleased;
no prefecture or commandery was permitted to compel him to serve as an abbot. Beating the drum to take leave of the assembly, he spoke this verse: "Originally, I have no home."
"Guests, how can you bear to wander as you please? With the wind at our backs, we ply our oars and poles; the boatman shall descend upon Yangzhou.
Having departed the capital, the carriages and horses of princes, dukes, and nobles followed one after another in a continuous stream. As he was about to part, the Master instructed them, saying:

"The passage of time cannot be toyed with; old age and sickness do not wait for anyone. Strive only in diligent cultivation without indolence—this is true assistance. Those who heard this were moved beyond measure.
He did not shed tears. Later, he resided at Lingyan. Those who inherited his Dharma and transmitted his Way numbered more than a hundred.
Entering the hall, he said: "When the great sound is once split open, heaven and earth are shaken. When the laws and regulations are put into practice, the myriad functions are suddenly pared away.
The paths of sage and ordinary are cut off; the sentiments of Buddhas and patriarchs are forgotten. At this moment, east and west cannot be distinguished, nor can north and south be divided. From...
The teaching remains dark and vast through a thousand ages and ten thousand ages. To fill the ditches and block the ravines—no one understands.
(He plants his staff upright. He descends from the seat. Ascending the hall: Nothing is more precipitous than the peak of Kukkutapāda; when travelers reach this point, the path is difficult to pass.
Only fearing that those who are disciples under the Patriarch’s gate will not move even a hair’s breadth to enter therein. Examine!
Ascending the hall, he said: "To question is not an offense; to answer is likewise without fault. Why? Because gaining it does not make one first, and losing it does not make one last.
If you penetrate this principle, why discuss emptiness or existence? Since time immemorial, the thousand sages have been thus at ease. Let the sun and moon race each other as they will;
formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness pass in the snap of a finger. Gain and loss, right and wrong—all are but a single mouth. *Duh!*
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Beside the Terrace of Gusu, one does not speak of spring or autumn; before the eyes of a patch-robed monk, how can one discuss the profound and the subtle?

One may simply wear robes and eat rice, playing with the water and gazing at the mountains. Seeing stars at night and seeing the sun by day, holding the plow with both hands while the water rises above the knees—this is exactly what was prophesied on Vulture Peak. Through kalpas, has it ever been different from today?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Upon the tip of a single hair, one manifests the Jewel-King lands; sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Holding up his staff, he said: "This is a mote of dust. How do you explain the principle of turning the Dharma Wheel?
Today, this mountain monk will not spare his eyebrows to explain it through for all of you. When it is held up, the waters of the ocean surge into waves, and Mount Sumeru..."
"Jigaba! Put it down! The four seas are peaceful and clear; heaven and earth are solemn and still. I dare ask you all: tell me, is it when you pick it up? Or is it when you put it down?
"To hesitate when one must decide—this is a double case. [He strikes the meditation seat and descends.]

On the first day of the first month of the year, a monk asked, "When a thousand lamps illuminate one another and the sounds of stringed and wind instruments intermingle—right at such a time, where is the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Thank you for your offering. The monk said, "Is this not your way of benefiting people? The Master said, "It is very much like coming to a feast without having fasted."
Question: "Above is heaven and below is earth; I do not yet understand what substance lies between them. The Master said: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
[The student] said: "If that is so, I thank the Master for his answer. The Master said: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers. [The student] said: "How can you deceive people, Reverend?"
He said, "This is rather the fault of this old monk.
[The student] asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He said, "Han Xin facing the throne. [The student] asked, "How does one understand this?
He said, "Ten thousand corpses lie across the land; had I known what would happen today, I would have regretted not being cautious in the beginning. He said, "... (The master remained silent).
The weeds grow lush upon the tombs of the Three Sovereigns.
Question: "The spring wind blows through the ancient trees; the setting sun descends the front mountains. What is the meaning of 'non-transmigration'? He said:
"Who cares for your idle affairs on the green mountains? Within the marketplace of the white days, there are people of their own."
Question: "Whose song does the Master sing? Whose lineage of the school’s wind does he succeed? He replied: "The tune is ancient and the spirit is pure; the wind naturally rises high.
His appearance is haggard and his bones are stern, so people pay him no heed. [The questioner] said: "If that is so, then you are the son of Jianfu and the direct grandson of Xuedou.
He replied: "I suspect you have not yet grasped where this leads."
Question: "What is the white ox in the open field? Answer: "Let it loose; there is no place to seek it. Question:
"From where was that news just now obtained? Answer: "It fits."
Question: "I know that you have long harbored a treasure within your bag; today, on this stage, I ask you to let me borrow it for a moment.
He replied, "Why must it be so? (From the *Pudeng lu*).
Ascending the hall, he said: "Look! Look! A brilliant, auspicious light shines, illuminating the great trichiliocosm.

Ten billion lands as numerous as motes of dust, ten billion oceans, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion sets of four continents—even down to lands as small as motes of dust—all appear simultaneously within this light. Do you all see it, worthy ones? If you do see it..."
"I grant it. I allow you that your parents are at Rui Guang. If you do not see them, do not say that Rui Guang does not shine its light upon you.
Examine this! Ascending the hall, he said: "The head is round like heaven; the feet are square like earth. With an ancient countenance of imposing majesty, such is the spirit of a man of worth.
He kicks over Mount Sumeru and tramples the waters of the ocean, leaving Indra and the Dragon King with no place to stand. Then, picking up his staff, he said:
He comes back and evades on his staff. "Tut! No matter what supernatural powers or transformations you may employ, in the end you must return here.
He strikes the ground once with the staff. (The above from the *Huìyuán*).
Upon arriving at Rui Guang Temple, he gathered the assembly and struck the drum; however, the drum repeatedly fell away, spinning and vibrating with a great roar.
The crowd was startled, but a monk stepped forward and cried out, "This is an auspicious omen that the Dharma-thunder of this Master shall shake the earth! Suddenly, the monk vanished from sight.
From that time on, the Dharma assemblies flourished daily until the congregation reached five hundred people.
While he resided at Ruiwang Temple, there was a man who butchered oxen; one ox escaped and ran back to him, kneeling as if to plead its case. He then purchased it and kept it as a pet.

While he resided at Jingci Temple, there was a great drought; the lakes and wells were all exhausted. In the western corner of the monastery, a sweet spring gushed forth spontaneously, and golden eels were caught.
He therefore dredged it to form a well and cast the fish into its depths. Although the monastic community numbered over a thousand people, they drew water from it without it ever running dry.
A woman of the Zhang family had a daughter who died. She dreamed that her mother said to her, "I have become a snake due to my transgressions.
Upon waking, she found a snake beneath the coffin. She took it to the Master Ben, who then preached the Dharma for her. He returned the snake to its original place;
shortly thereafter, a black cicada flew over the coffin and the snake vanished. The mother made a vow, saying, "If you are indeed my daughter, you shall enter this cage," and she took hold of it.

He visited Jingci Temple again, where [the nun] fulfilled her vow as requested. Ben then preached the Dharma for her once more. That evening, she dreamed of the woman saying, "The two retributions have already been liberated.
Her manifestations of supernatural power were extraordinary in this manner as well (as recorded above in the *Sengbao zhuan*).
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yuánfú era, the Master bathed and lay down.

His disciples stood in a circle around him and requested a verse, entreating him to rise and sit upright so that he might transform both monastics and laypeople. The Master gazed at them intently and said, "Fools!
I am usually too lazy to compose verses; what is the point of making a special effort today? When I wish to lie down, I simply lie down. It cannot be otherwise now."

On the day he passed away, he sat upright in meditation. Taking up his brush, he wrote in large characters: "My final affairs are entrusted to Shou-rong. He then cast aside his brush and slept soundly until his passing.

When the common people and officials offered incense for the funeral rites, the flame continued to burn for an entire month. By imperial decree, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the upper section of the temple.
He lived for eighty years and spent fifty-two summer retreats in seclusion. His posthumous title was Fakan, and his stupa was named Rui-guang (Continued Lamp History).
It is said that he passed away while seated (the aforementioned *Pudeng*).
Emperor Zhezong conferred upon him the honorary title of Chan Master; the Imperial Uncle, Prince Jing, personally carried the imperial edict to bestow it upon him.
The *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) praises him, saying: "When Zhenggong Fu resided in Luoyang, he saw Yuanrong at Huayan Temple and recorded Yuanben’s words."
He sent a verse to him, saying: "Because I saw Master Yong, my realization has deepened; Through successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Great Teacher.
Though one may speak of the vast distance of rivers and mountains between the southeast and here, I face the Holy Light and the Sublime Sound directly before my eyes.
Wang Xianmu Han first saw Ben ascend the seat and look about with his eyes, whereupon he realized his own original mind. I have heard it said that when Maitreya was in the world, the multitude...
The excellence of his mind of form-born [wisdom] was such that when he uttered a single perfect sound, beings understood it according to their own kind.

Although more than two thousand years have passed since the Buddha’s era, he was able to cause kings, dukes, and nobles to awaken upon hearing his reputation and to realize the truth upon beholding his countenance;

from this, one may know those who followed him constantly and were personally refined by him. Thus, while there were eighty-odd people in Jiangxi, those at the root [of his lineage] were twice as many.

The flourishing of the transmission of the Dharma in recent times has been unsurpassed; were it not for his vow to propagate the Way of the Dharma and his practice that accorded with the Buddha’s mind, how could he have reached such a state? (From the *Sengbao zhuan*)
